steps.label: Statements
steps.body: Rational Choice Theory: The reason various political parties are popular is that individual voters make a deliberate decision to support the party they think has policies that will yield them the greatest economic advantage. Many Sociologists: This theory is wrong. A complex phenomenon such as the rise of a political organization cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Match up the parts of the sociologists' response. The theory says that X (popular support for political parties) is explained by Y (individual voters deliberately backing the party whose policies they think will give them the greatest economic advantage). The sociologists object that a complex phenomenon cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

That objection only lands if Y is a simple phenomenon. If voters' economic decisions were themselves complex, the sociologists' rule would not touch the theory. So the sociologists apparently assume that Y is simple.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer saying the sociologists treat voters' economically driven decisions as a simple phenomenon, or at least as something that isn't automatically complex.

The stem asks what the sociologists believe, so we can only credit them with what their objection commits them to. A modestly worded answer ("need not," "can be") is easier to prove than a sweeping one.

notes.body:
This is the belief the objection runs on. The sociologists reject the theory because a complex phenomenon can't be caused by a simple one. That only counts against rational-choice theory if the cause the theory names, voters' economically motivated decisions, is simple. So the sociologists must think those decisions are not necessarily complex. "Need not constitute a complex phenomenon" says exactly that, and says it modestly.

The move: when a group rejects a theory by citing a general rule, ask which category the rule must put the theory's key idea in. That classification is something the group has to believe.

The sociologists' rule only rules one thing out: a simple cause can't produce a complex result. It says nothing about how many causes a complex phenomenon has, or that each of them must be complex. A single complex cause would fit their rule just as well. "Many complex causes" adds a claim about number that we can't trace to anything the sociologists said.

The sociologists never say what does cause popular support for parties. They only say the theory's cause is too simple. Religion and culture never appear in the passage, so we have no basis for crediting the sociologists with this view.

This is the reverse of what they believe. Their rule is about complex phenomena, so the objection only applies if popular support for parties is complex. If they thought it was never complex, their own rule wouldn't touch the theory and the objection would collapse.

The sociologists don't deny that voters care about economic advantage. They deny that those decisions are enough, by themselves, to explain something as complex as the rise of a political organization. Someone can agree that voters chase economic advantage and still think it's too simple a cause.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by reducing the monitoring done by managers, as long as the employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by giving their employees expensive bonuses.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: To reach this conclusion about the employees at these particular corporations, we need to assume that there is a relationship between giving them strong incentives to keep working hard and giving them expensive bonuses. We have to assume that these bonuses would motivate them to keep working hard even when the managers aren't watching them closely.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the bridge between "strong incentives" in the evidence and "expensive bonuses" in the conclusion: expensive bonuses work as strong incentives for these employees. Negate that, and the evidence's condition is never met by the bonuses, so nothing connects the bonuses to any savings and the conclusion loses its support.

Watch for two traps: an answer that makes bonuses the only way to save, and an answer that explains why the plan would work if it already worked.

notes.body: The argument is about what highly profitable corporations can do, not about how many corporations do it now. Negate A: many corporations give bonuses strong enough to keep employees working hard without monitoring. That doesn't hurt the argument at all, so the argument doesn't depend on A.

B explains why savings would happen: if bonuses save money, it's because they cut monitoring time. The argument only needs bonuses to be able to save money, not a claim about the reason behind every case of savings. Negate B: a corporation could save money with bonuses for some other reason. The conclusion still holds, since it only says the corporations can save money.

C is about whether these corporations actually have managers monitor much. The argument is about what they could save by reducing monitoring. Negate C: more valuable manager time doesn't make monitoring less likely. That fits the argument fine. Monitoring is still costly, and cutting it while keeping employees motivated still saves money.

This connects the two terms the argument swaps. The evidence says these corporations can save money by reducing monitoring, as long as employees get strong incentives. The conclusion says they can save money by giving expensive bonuses. D says expensive bonuses are strong incentives for exactly these employees. Negate it: the bonuses aren't strong incentives. Then the evidence's condition isn't met, and nothing in the argument shows the bonuses save any money.

The move: when the conclusion names a specific tool (expensive bonuses) and the evidence names a general requirement (strong incentives), the argument assumes the tool meets the requirement.

E is too strong. "Only if" makes expensive bonuses a requirement for any savings from reduced monitoring. The argument needs bonuses to be one way to supply strong incentives, not the only way. Negate E: a corporation could cut monitoring and save money using other incentives, like promotions. Bonuses could still work too, so the argument stands.
